7514693906400473092.author: Augustin Sayer
7514693906400473092.text:
Ownership is overrated.

Had Matt Logan, co-founder and GP at Earthshot Ventures, on episode 17 of Fault Lines and this one stuck with me. Most VCs obsess over owning 15-20% of a company. Matt's take is that at the end of the day what matters is your cash-on-cash multiple, not what percentage you own. If you really believe the upside is $100B and not $1B, being at 1% or even a tenth of a percent is totally fine.

Their two biggest positions, KoBold Metals and Etched, both started as smaller initial stakes. Etched just raised at $21B... kind of proves the point.

Architects and investors are both asking whether an ASIC can beat the GPU. After 2 decades in memory and silicon design, I think that’s the wrong question. 

Will specialized ASICs dethrone the GPU in AI inference? The better question is: which part of inference?

Etched’s Sohu has reignited the debate. Hardwire the transformer into silicon, strip out the general-purpose overhead, and cost per token and tokens per watt can improve dramatically. The funding and customer commitments show the market takes the thesis seriously.

But three things will decide the outcome, and none of them is peak FLOPS.

7514895488425418752.author: RSV Global LLC FZ
7514895488425418752.text:
The most consequential pattern in AI this week was not a capability announcement. It was the structure of accountability.

The UK Information Commissioner's Office got 10 AI firms to pledge data-protection changes on October 8. On October 9, it opened a six-week public inquiry to understand what agentic AI is and what data it processes. The regulator is simultaneously certifying compliance and gathering the evidence needed to define it. The pledges are not a governance mechanism. They are a placeholder for one.

The White House AI accord, signed September 29, has the same structure at a different scale. Signatories include OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, xAI, and Nvidia. No auditor is named

7514940066675253248.author: Muhammad Yaser
7514940066675253248.text:
A chip startup just doubled to $40 billion in three weeks.

Etched designs custom AI chips built for one job: running large language models, faster and cheaper than the GPUs everyone rents.

Weeks after raising at a $21 billion valuation, investors are now fielding offers at $40 to $50 billion. Four years old. One 10-megawatt data center in Silicon Valley. No chip you can buy yet.

Here is the bold claim. The AI race stopped being about who trains the smartest model. It is about who owns the machines that answer your questions, and inference chips are the new oil.

So the question: when AI answers get cheap enough to be free, who makes money, the model or the silicon underneath it?

7515003312098799616.author: Sergio Vital
7515003312098799616.text:
One developer cloned seven Adobe apps with AI last week and gave them all away for free.

Your feed is going to tell you software is over. It is not. But something did just change, and it is not the thing people are celebrating.

What happened: Brandon Thomas, an engineer with about fifteen years of experience and a decade in Rust, released Artcraft. Seven open source apps mirroring Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, Lightroom, After Effects, InDesign and Acrobat Pro. Built in Rust with AI assisted reverse engineering. His motivation was Adobe's cancellation fees, the same practice behind the $150M settlement Adobe agreed to in March while denying wrongdoing. His summary: "software is over."
